findings.paper_title: Item 10 Audit Report and Opinion GPAC 16.7.26
findings.headline: Staff capacity constraints and outdated procedures identified as systemic issues
findings.detail: Internal audit identified persistent cross-council themes including staff capacity challenges causing audit delays or inability to complete full scopes, lack of up-to-date policies and procedures, system limitations requiring manual workarounds, and persistent control failures (e.g., school payroll miscoding, unmanaged asset registers). One audit was carried over to 2026/27 due to staff absence on ill health grounds.
findings.matters: Staffing shortages and system limitations increase operational risk, error potential, and resilience concerns. They suggest the council may be under-resourced to maintain effective financial and operational controls, which affects credit quality.
findings.figures: Common themes included staff absence causing audit delays; no quantified staffing levels provided
findings.quote: Staff capacity challenges which cause delays in work undertaken or the inability to undertake full scopes of work

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Audit Report and Opinion GPAC 16.7.26
findings.headline: Only 47% of prior audit recommendations fully implemented within a year
findings.detail: Follow-up testing of 32 prior-year recommendations found only 47% (15 audits) fully implemented, 44% partially implemented, and 9% with no evidence of action. Even Priority 1 (urgent) recommendations showed weak implementation, with only 2 of 3 fully completed.
findings.matters: Low implementation of audit recommendations indicates either that management lacks capacity to address known control weaknesses or does not prioritize them. Either situation suggests systemic governance concerns that could affect financial controls and service delivery.
findings.figures: 47% (15) fully implemented, 44% (14) partially implemented, with 2 Priority 1 recommendations and 1 of 3 Priority 1 recommendations fully implemented
findings.quote: Of the recommendations tested, 47% (15) were fully implemented (of which 2 were Priority 1) and 44% were partially implemented (of which 1 was a Priority 1).

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Audit Report and Opinion GPAC 16.7.26
findings.headline: Limited assurance opinions increased from 27% to 42% of audits year-on-year
findings.detail: In 2025/26, 42% of general assurance reviews received 'limited assurance' ratings (meaning significant weaknesses requiring improvement), compared to 27% in 2024/25. Simultaneously, 'substantial assurance' opinions fell from 9% to 4%, showing fewer areas of strong control across the council.
findings.matters: Deteriorating audit opinion trends suggest the council's control environment is weakening rather than improving. This negative trajectory is a red flag for lenders assessing the council's governance maturity.
findings.figures: 2025/26: 4% Substantial, 54% Reasonable, 42% Limited; 2024/25: 9% Substantial, 64% Reasonable, 27% Limited
findings.quote: As a percentage % / Year Substantial Reasonable Limited No / 2025/26 4% 54% 42% 0% / 2024/25 9% 64% 27% 0%

findings.paper_title: Item 10 Audit Report and Opinion GPAC 16.7.26
findings.headline: Audit opinion was borderline between reasonable and limited assurance
findings.detail: The council received a 'reasonable' overall audit opinion on its governance, risk management, and control arrangements for 2025/26. However, the report explicitly states the opinion was 'borderline with the limited opinion,' meaning a small number of additional weaknesses would have triggered a downgrade to limited assurance, which signals significant control gaps.
findings.matters: A borderline opinion indicates the council's control environment is adequate but fragile. For lenders, this suggests governance structures are on the edge of acceptability; any material deterioration could result in a limited opinion, which would be a material warning sign.
findings.figures: The opinion was borderline with limited assurance
findings.quote: The opinion was borderline with the limited opinion.

findings.paper_title: Item 9 GP + Audit Committee 29 July 2026 LGA Finance peer challenge Final report
findings.headline: New section 151 officer appointed but not yet in post at time of review; arrival expected to strengthen financial grip
findings.detail: The peer team noted that the arrival of the new section 151 officer (appointed but not in post at the time of the FPC) will provide stability and strengthen the financial services team and bring a renewed focus on structure and governance. This leadership transition is material for financial management continuity.
findings.matters: A lender should track whether the new CFO brings the financial discipline and strategic capability needed to execute the council's multi-year financial plan; leadership changes at this level are material to credit risk
findings.figures: new section 151 officer appointed at the time of review but not yet in post
findings.quote: the arrival of the new section 151 officer (appointed but not in post at the time of the FPC) will provide stability and strengthen the financial services team and will bring a renewed focus on structure and governance

findings.paper_title: Item 9 GP + Audit Committee 29 July 2026 LGA Finance peer challenge Final report
findings.headline: General Fund reserves remain low, creating ongoing reliance on transformation delivery
findings.detail: The progress review acknowledges that un-ringfenced reserves as a percentage of net revenue expenditure remain amongst the lowest of London boroughs, even after increases from previous years. This necessitates the transformation programme being successful. The council is proposing to add £0.5m to reserves from 2026/27 onwards, but the pace of replenishment is slow relative to the scale of the challenge.
findings.matters: Low reserves reduce the council's ability to manage unexpected pressures or delays in transformation delivery; a lender faces heightened refinancing risk if the council hits an unplanned shortfall
findings.figures: Un-ringfenced reserves as a percentage of net revenue expenditure are amongst the lowest of all London boroughs; Council has proposed £0.5m is added to reserves from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: The Council recognises it has a relatively low level of General Fund reserves, even though these have been increased from previous years, which necessitates the transformation programme being successful

findings.paper_title: Item 9 GP + Audit Committee 29 July 2026 LGA Finance peer challenge Final report
findings.headline: Children's Services transformation programme now linked to MTFS, with Department for Education funding supporting 30% of transformation costs
findings.detail: The council has developed a dedicated Children's Services transformation plan aligned with the MTFS. A dedicated finance lead was appointed in August 2025 to strengthen business case development. Transformation savings will be incorporated into MTFS reporting from January 2026. Department for Education funding is earmarked for these reforms, with approximately 30% of 2025–26 funding expected to support transformation costs.
findings.matters: Children's Services has historically been a significant source of overspend (29.9% in 2023/24); this structured approach and external funding support suggests movement towards control of this risk
findings.figures: approximately 30 per cent of the 2025–26 funding expected to support transformation costs
findings.quote: A dedicated finance lead was appointed in August 2025 to strengthen business case development and financial oversight. Transformation savings will be incorporated into MTFS reporting from January 2026, with six-monthly Cabinet updates ensuring transparency

findings.paper_title: Item 9 GP + Audit Committee 29 July 2026 LGA Finance peer challenge Final report
findings.headline: SEND Safety Valve deficit exceeds agreed assumption by £3.872m
findings.detail: Bexley's Dedicated Schools Grant accumulated deficit at 31 March 2025 is projected to reach £11.513m, significantly higher than the £7.641m assumed in the Safety Valve agreement with the Department for Education. The agreed deliverables are not yet on track. This matters because it indicates the council is falling behind on a statutory reform commitment with direct implications for school funding.
findings.matters: A lender should know that the council has a material variance against a DfE-backed commitment, which could trigger further intervention or closer monitoring by central government
findings.figures: accumulated deficit on 31 March 2025 will be £11.513m, compared to an assumed deficit in Safety Valve of £7.641m
findings.quote: The SEND safety valve agreed deliverables are not yet on track, but hard work is being done on the agreed changes, and they are starting to have an impact

findings.paper_title: Item 9 GP + Audit Committee 29 July 2026 LGA Finance peer challenge Final report
findings.headline: Budget gap remains substantial despite transformation: £8.192m in 2027/28 rising to £21.885m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The council faces a significant medium-term budget deficit even with transformation savings factored in. The progress review recognises that while transformation is a valuable short-term tool, the council must develop a broader economic growth strategy to address longer-term financial pressures. The gap grows substantially over the MTFS period.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that the council has a credible, multi-faceted plan to close a gap of this scale; transformation savings alone will not close it, and the plan beyond transformation is not detailed in this paper
findings.figures: £8.192 million in 2027/28, increasing to £21.885 million by 2030/31
findings.quote: the Transformation Programme is recognised as a valuable tool for delivering savings in the short term, but that work is also underway to develop a broader economic growth strategy to address longer-term financial pressures

findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 Appendix 1 RIsk Register 19.7.26
findings.headline: Council has recently been subject to Government intervention and faces rigorous inspection regime
findings.detail: Bexley is under active Government intervention and must now meet increasingly rigorous inspection requirements including the new CQC local authority assessment framework. Poor inspection outcomes could trigger statutory improvement notices and impact future funding.
findings.matters: Recent Government intervention indicates the council faced prior financial or governance difficulties; ongoing regulatory scrutiny carries risk of future funding impacts.
findings.figures: None provided in this risk register
findings.quote: The Council has recently been subject to Government intervention and must now demonstrate its ability to meet the requirements of an increasingly rigorous inspection regime.

findings.paper_title: Item 12.1 Appendix 1 RIsk Register 19.7.26
findings.headline: Increasing MTFS budget gap threatens the Council's ability to set a balanced budget
findings.detail: The Council flags an increasing gap between planned spending and available resources, driven by rising service demands, increasing unit costs, vulnerable economic climate, uncertain future funding, new unfunded burdens, and uncertain delivery of the transformation programme. The register identifies specific risk of inability to set a balanced budget and potential requirement for exceptional financial support or S114 part 3 report.
findings.matters: A council unable to balance its budget requires exceptional Government intervention; a S114 report signals severe financial distress.
findings.figures: None provided in this risk register
findings.quote: The Council has a legal duty to deliver a balanced budget but there is an increasing MTFS budget gap due to challenges including: Increasing levels of demands for services and increasing complexity of services provided. Increasing unit costs. A vulnerable economic climate and uncertainty on future funding.

findings.paper_title: Item 8 LBB Treasury Outturn Report 2025-26 Final for GPAC
findings.headline: Council reduced long-term debt by £6m while generating £1.505m in treasury investment income
findings.detail: Despite the challenging interest rate environment, Bexley made debt repayments of £6.031m and generated positive treasury income of £1.505m, with £1.324m from money market funds and £0.181m from pooled property funds, contributing to overall financial resilience.
findings.matters: Demonstrates that the council is reducing leverage and generating offsetting returns from cash management, both positive indicators of financial health, debt service capacity, and active treasury management.
findings.figures: Long-term debt repayment: £6.031m; treasury income: £1.505m (£1.324m from MMF, £0.181m from pooled funds); total debt reduced from £230.615m to £224.584m
findings.quote: For 202 5/26, the council received £ 1.505m treasury income from its investments. Interest received was generated by MMFs (£ 1.324m), fixed term deposits (£0.001m) and pooled property funds (£0.181m).

findings.paper_title: Item 8 LBB Treasury Outturn Report 2025-26 Final for GPAC
findings.headline: Council took £25m in short-term borrowing at 5.97% to manage liquidity while deferring long-term borrowing decisions
findings.detail: Bexley borrowed £25m as temporary short-term loans (Feb-March 2026) at an average rate of 5.97% to manage cash flow needs. This represents a tactical decision to accept higher temporary borrowing costs rather than lock in current long-term PWLB rates, suggesting the council expects rates may become more favorable.
findings.matters: Reveals the council's market timing judgment about future interest rates and demonstrates active treasury management; for a lender, it shows sophisticated financial forecasting but also depends on rates improving.
findings.figures: £25m short-term borrowing at 5.97% average rate vs PWLB long-term rates of 5.92%-6.50% depending on maturity
findings.quote: Short term loans are taken to manage cash flow / liquidity requirements

findings.paper_title: Item 8 LBB Treasury Outturn Report 2025-26 Final for GPAC
findings.headline: PWLB borrowing rates have risen significantly, increasing the cost of funding capital projects
findings.detail: The Public Works Loan Board's certainty rates have increased substantially across all maturities compared to March 2025, with the 30-year rate rising from 5.99% to 6.50%. The council explicitly notes this increase is driven by inflation, elevated energy prices, and geopolitical risks, directly impacting the cost of financing the council's capital investment program.
findings.matters: Rising borrowing costs affect a council's ability to fund capital projects affordably and service debt; a lender needs to assess impact on project returns, and a finance director needs to plan investment decisions around higher financing costs.
findings.quote: There has been an increase in Certainty Rates for 2026 compared to the prior year, primarily driven by inflation, elevated global energy prices, political uncertainty and geopolitical risks.

findings.paper_title: 1 Budget Monitor March 2026 - Outturn (Public Cabinet)
findings.headline: SEN Transport overspent £1.243m and Educational Psychology staffing overspent £0.503m on expensive agency cover
findings.detail: SEN Transport overspend of £1.243m driven by: £0.595m from DfE ruling that personal transport budget costs cannot be charged to Dedicated Schools Grant, plus faster than expected growth in numbers accessing transport reflecting significant growth in Education Health and Care Plans. Education staffing £0.503m overspend from expensive agency cover for Educational Psychologist posts and historic gap between budget and cost of establishment. 2026/27 budget includes additional education staffing funding and recruitment/retention strategy for Educational Psychologists.
findings.matters: Structural staffing shortages in critical SEND support roles are driving high agency costs and raising questions about service quality and cost containment in vulnerable child protection.
findings.figures: SEN Transport overspend £1.243m; Education staffing overspend £0.503m; DfE ruling cost £0.595m
findings.quote: The main cost pressure was £1.243m in SEN Transport. £0.595m of the overspend was due to the ruling from the Department for Education that costs of personal transport budgets could not be charged to the Dedicated Schools Grant.

findings.paper_title: 1 Budget Monitor March 2026 - Outturn (Public Cabinet)
findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £5.833m (13.47%) including £3.823m BexleyCo scheme and Erith regeneration delays
findings.detail: Capital outturn £37.464m against revised budget of £43.297m. Finance and Corporate underspent £3.823m primarily from BexleyCo development scheme not completing by year-end. Places & Communities slipped £0.996m including £0.428m on Erith Regeneration due to delays across multiple sites. Additions of £0.724m (mostly grant funding for EV charging) offset some slippage.
findings.matters: Material delays in major regeneration and housing schemes signal project delivery risk and may impact economic growth, housing supply, and future revenue benefits from these investments.
findings.figures: Total capital slippage £5.833m (13.47%); BexleyCo £3.823m; Erith Regeneration £0.428m; total capital outturn £37.464m vs budget £43.297m
findings.quote: Finance and Corporate have outturned at £13.027m against a revised budget of £16.850m. Total slippage of £3.823m is mostly driven by one site part of the BexleyCo scheme that did not complete by the end of the financial year.

findings.paper_title: 1 Budget Monitor March 2026 - Outturn (Public Cabinet)
findings.headline: General Fund bad debt provision increased £1.537m, with underlying deterioration of £5.456m when adjusted for write-offs
findings.detail: Bad debt provision rose from £10.732m (31 March 2025) to £12.269m (31 March 2026). Underlying increase of £5.456m when adjusted for £3.919m of debts written off during the year. Parking debt is significant component of increase. Council Tax collection shortfall (94.82% vs 95.51% target) and Business Rates collection 96.92% vs 97.07% target reflect cost-of-living pressures on residents and business difficulties.
findings.matters: Growing bad debt provision signals deteriorating collection rates and resident/business financial stress, reducing reliable income generation despite improving cash collection relative to charge growth.
findings.figures: Bad debt provision increased £1.537m to £12.269m; underlying increase £5.456m; Council Tax collection 94.82% (0.69% below target); Business Rates 96.92% (0.15% below target)
findings.quote: The outturn position shows that the General Fund bad debt provision increased by £1.537m, from £10.732m to £12.269m. However, when adjusted for debts written off against the provision during the year, the underlying movement represents an overall increase of £5.456m.

findings.paper_title: 1 Budget Monitor March 2026 - Outturn (Public Cabinet)
findings.headline: Council increased borrowing by £20.984m to £249.584m, including £25m temporary loans at 5.97%
findings.detail: Total council borrowing increased from £230.615m (31 March 2025) to £249.584m (31 March 2026). This includes £25.000m in temporary loans taken at weighted average 5.97%, with PWLB borrowing reduced £4.016m. Weighted average rate on total borrowing is 3.60%. Borrowing undertaken to support liquidity requirements and cash flow management during the year.
findings.matters: Increasing reliance on temporary borrowing at high interest rates signals cash flow pressures and rising debt service costs that could constrain future spending flexibility.
findings.figures: Total borrowing increased £20.984m; temporary loans £25.000m at 5.97%; total outstanding £249.584m; average rate 3.60%
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Council undertook additional borrowing to support liquidity requirements and cash flow management. Overall borrowing increased by £20.984m during the year, from £230.615m as at 31 March 2025 to £249.584m as at 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 1 Budget Monitor March 2026 - Outturn (Public Cabinet)
findings.headline: Adult Social Care placement activity overran by 322 placements, creating £6.154m overspend against plan
findings.detail: Planned 3,224 placements but actual activity was 3,546, a 9.9% overspend on volume. The budget for placement activity is based on average unit cost per week. This activity overrun resulted in a £6.154m overspend. Partially mitigated by Health grants (£2.977m) and client contributions (£0.993m). Service implemented Financial Intervention Strategy with £3.260m mitigations. Directorate overall overspend £3.771m, increased £0.150m since January forecast.
findings.matters: Demographic and demand-driven overspend indicates sustained pressure from aging population and rising care complexity that will continue into future years, threatening budget sustainability.
findings.figures: 3,546 actual placements vs 3,224 budgeted; £6.154m overspend; £3.771m directorate overspend
findings.quote: The budget for placement activity is based on the average unit cost per week that allows for 3,224 placements across all types of care. The activity for the year was 3,546, 322 more than planned. The increase has resulted in an overspend of £6.154m.

findings.paper_title: 1 Budget Monitor March 2026 - Outturn (Public Cabinet)
findings.headline: Accumulated High Needs Block deficit reached £22.495m with unfunded 10% liability of £1.710m after Safety Valve ends
findings.detail: High Needs overspend of £5.178m on top of budgeted deficit of £5.893m totals £11.071m annual deficit. The accumulated deficit at 31 March 2026 is £22.495m. The government's new High Needs Stability Grant will fund 90% (£20.786m), leaving Bexley to fund 10% (£1.710m) of the accumulated deficit. Safety Valve programme closes April 2026. The 2026/27 budget now shows an in-year deficit of £22.473m pending further government support.
findings.matters: This is a structural and growing demand pressure that creates a contingent liability on the council's balance sheet and raises questions about service sustainability for vulnerable children with special educational needs.
findings.figures: Accumulated deficit £22.495m; annual deficit £11.071m; unfunded liability £1.710m; 2026/27 deficit £22.473m
findings.quote: The final position for the year is an overspend on High Needs Block budgets of £5.178m, in addition to a budgeted deficit of £5.893m. The total High Needs deficit for the year is therefore £11.071m, a reduction of £0.957m compared to the January 2026 forecast.

findings.paper_title: 1 Medium Term Financial Strategy -July 2026 - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Soft plastics collection mandate by March 2027 with unquantified cost
findings.detail: Local Authorities must implement soft plastics packaging collection at kerbside by 31 March 2027. Bexley does not currently collect these materials. Paper notes: 'It is very likely that there will be additional costs associated with the collection and disposal of this material' but no cost estimate is provided. Treated as unfunded mandate risk.
findings.matters: This is a statutory requirement with no allocated funding and estimated costs not yet built into MTFS. It represents unfunded pressure in 2026/27 ahead of a period of already-identified deficits.
findings.figures: Mandate date: 31 March 2027
findings.quote: It is a requirement that Local Authorities in England must have in place by 31 March 2027 the service provision to collect soft plastics packaging at the kerbside. Bexley does not currently collect these materials, and further investigation is required in to how these can be collected. It is very likely that there will be additional costs associated with the collection and disposal of this material.

findings.paper_title: 1 Medium Term Financial Strategy -July 2026 - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Capital receipts of £9.6m planned for 2026/27; delays would require additional borrowing
findings.detail: Council plans capital receipts of £9.609m in 2026/27 to fund capital programme and transformation. Only £0.777m is assumed in 2026/27 funding, but £2.1m is earmarked for transformation. Paper warns: 'If the planned disposals are delayed, then further borrowing may be necessary.'
findings.matters: Capital programme is already heavily dependent on borrowing (£204.954m of £248.115m total, or 82.6%). Any slip in planned asset sales would increase borrowing requirement and interest costs at a time when rates are high (PWLB 50-year rates at 6.32%).
findings.figures: £9.609m planned capital receipts; £204.954m of £248.115m capital programme funded by borrowing; PWLB 50-year rate: 6.32%
findings.quote: If the planned disposals are delayed, then further borrowing may be necessary.

findings.paper_title: 1 Medium Term Financial Strategy -July 2026 - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Fees and charges income below peer average; commercialisation workstream not yet quantified
findings.detail: Bexley's sales, fees and charges are 14.5% of gross expenditure, below nearest neighbour average of 18.8%. The Future Bexley commercialisation workstream is expected to increase fees and charges income, but 'current assumptions in the MTFS do not duplicate this workstream' and the uplift 'would be included in future reports.' This means budget gap may widen if commercialisation does not deliver.
findings.matters: Income generation is a lever for closing the budget gap, but it is not yet modelled in the MTFS. If commercialisation fails to deliver, the council will need alternative mitigations.
findings.figures: Current assumption: 14.5% of gross expenditure; peer average: 18.8%
findings.quote: As a proportion of gross expenditure total sales, fees and charges was 14.5%, which is below the nearest neighbour average of 18.8%. This applies to all service areas except Adult Social Care and Cultural and Related Services which have a slightly higher cost compared to the nearest neighbours.

findings.paper_title: 1 Medium Term Financial Strategy -July 2026 - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Reserve replenishment needed but 'opportunities are limited'
findings.detail: General fund reserves held at £14.360m across the MTFS period. The council explicitly states it 'is imperative that reserves are replenished in the short to medium term in order to improve financial resilience against future increasing uncertainty. However, opportunities are limited as this can only be achieved if the Council identify further saving, efficiency, transformational or income opportunities.'
findings.matters: Reserves are a key measure of financial resilience and borrowing capacity. A council at statutory minimum reserves with a growing budget gap and no identified mechanism to rebuild them signals deteriorating financial health.
findings.figures: General Fund Reserve: £14.360m (2027/28 - 2030/31, held flat)
findings.quote: It is imperative that reserves are replenished in the short to medium term in order to improve financial resilience against future increasing uncertainty. However, opportunities are limited as this can only be achieved if the Council identify further saving, efficiency, transformational or income opportunities.

findings.paper_title: 1 Medium Term Financial Strategy -July 2026 - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Adult and children's social care demand growing faster than assumed; pay award risk unresolved
findings.detail: The council reports 'increasing demand, higher unit costs, and greater competition' in Adults, Children's Social Care and SEN transport. The budget assumes 3.2% pay award, but the paper warns 'there remains a risk that pay awards may be higher than anticipated.' A 1% overshoot on pay across the MTFS period would add £3.807m to the budget gap.
findings.matters: These are the council's largest and fastest-growing spend areas. Demand risk is structural, not temporary. Unresolved NJC pay negotiations create additional downside risk at a time when the council is already predicting deficits.
findings.figures: Pay award sensitivity: +1% = £3.807m additional gap over MTFS; growth assumption sensitivity: +1% = £11.846m additional gap
findings.quote: In particular within Children's and Adult Social Care, SEN transport and Housing, the Council is seeing increasing demand, higher unit costs, and greater competition, because of changing market conditions.

findings.paper_title: 1 Medium Term Financial Strategy -July 2026 - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Schools high needs deficit could require £6.5m council contribution from March 2028
findings.detail: The Statutory Override for Dedicated Schools Grant ends April 2028. DfE will fund 90% of accumulated DSG deficit as at March 2026 via new High Needs Stability Grant. Bexley would be responsible for 10% of any unfunded deficit. The paper estimates this 'could amount to approx. £6.5m by March 2028' but notes 'it is difficult to quantify financial implications after March 2028.'
findings.matters: A sudden £6.5m call on reserves or budget in 2028/29 would materially worsen Bexley's financial position at a time when its general fund reserve is already only £14.360m. This is a known liability with an imminent cliff-edge.
findings.figures: £6.5m potential call on council budget from March 2028 onwards
findings.quote: If the Government continues the approach of expecting Local Authorities to pick up 10% of any deficit, this could amount to approx. £6.5m by March 2028.

findings.paper_title: 1 Medium Term Financial Strategy -July 2026 - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Contract inflation provision may be insufficient to cover actual cost increases
findings.detail: The council spends 57.28% of its budget on supplies and services and third-party contracts. Latest agreed inflation increases have already exceeded current provision. The MTFS sets aside £4.460m for 2027/28, but forecasted to £17.916m by 2030/31. The paper explicitly warns: if inflation assumptions increase by just 1%, the budget gap widens by £5.972m over the period.
findings.matters: As a heavily outsourced council, Bexley has material exposure to contract renegotiation risk. The council admits it is 'still a risk' that it cannot negotiate inflation 'as set out above, or other inflation pressures for non-contract spend is not contained.'
findings.figures: 57.28% of budget on contracts; £4.460m provision 2027/28; £17.916m by 2030/31; sensitivity: +1% inflation = £5.972m additional gap
findings.quote: Most of the Council's contracts for goods and services that span more than one year contain inflation clauses. Latest agreed inflation increases have been higher than current rates of inflation and provision set aside. This is an increasingly difficult position to maintain through the Medium Term Financial Strategy period and is still a risk.

findings.paper_title: 1 Medium Term Financial Strategy -July 2026 - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Growing budget deficit from £8.2m to £21.9m across four-year period
findings.detail: The council faces a budget gap of £8.192m for 2027/28, increasing to £21.885m by 2030/31. This represents a 167% increase in the cumulative gap over the MTFS period. The council must set a balanced budget by March 2027 but has not yet identified savings sufficient to close this gap.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can deliver a sustainable budget without service cuts that might affect delivery or borrowing capacity. The widening gap suggests structural issues beyond one-year pressures.
findings.quote: The council now has a budget gap of £8.192m for 2027/28, noting a budget gap still remains in future years estimated at £21.885m in 2030/31.

findings.paper_title: 5 - Schools budget 2025-26 outturn
findings.headline: Five maintained schools in deficit continuing into 2026-27
findings.detail: Five maintained schools closed the year in deficit and will remain so in 2026-27. Total maintained school balances fell 6% year on year from £2.139m to £2.114m. While the council offers support, these schools represent financial trouble that will require intervention.
findings.matters: Individual school deficits compound system-wide pressure and signal governance or resource management issues at school level that require ongoing council subsidy or intervention.
findings.figures: Five schools in deficit. Total maintained balances £2.114m (down from £2.139m).
findings.quote: five schools closed with a deficit balance and will continue to be in deficit in 2026-27. The Council offers advice and support in this situation.

findings.paper_title: 5 - Schools budget 2025-26 outturn
findings.headline: Independent sector and tuition placements driving high needs cost overruns
findings.detail: Independent sector placements outturn at £9.147m against a budget of £5.771m (overspend £3.376m). Tuition and personal budgets spent £3.275m against budget of £1.653m (overspend £1.622m). Further Education and Supported Internships spent £3.631m against £2.658m budget (overspend £973k). These overruns appear demand-driven and are not one-off.
findings.matters: Demand-driven cost pressures in special needs that consume £5m+ of the total deficit will persist unless provision is managed differently or funding increases. This is the core structural problem.
findings.figures: Independent Sector: budget £5.771m, outturn £9.147m (overspend £3.376m). Tuition and Personal Budgets: budget £1.653m, outturn £3.275m (overspend £1.622m).
findings.quote: The main contributory factor to the adverse outturn was variations in high needs expenditure totalling £5.242, partly offset by an underspend of £1.049 on early years and smaller variances on the schools and central blocks.

findings.paper_title: 5 - Schools budget 2025-26 outturn
findings.headline: Accumulated DSG deficit of £22.495m, with persistent £10m+ annual overspends
findings.detail: The council budgeted for a £5.893m in-year deficit but recorded £10.099m (a £4.206m adverse variance). The deficit brought forward from prior years was £12.396m. High needs expenditure overran by £5.242m, with only a £1.049m early years surplus to offset it. The council is running structural deficits that accumulate year on year.
findings.matters: A £22.5m cumulative schools deficit with no visible reduction path is a material financial vulnerability. Lenders assess whether a council can function within its resources; persistent, growing deficits signal structural insolvency risk.
findings.figures: Deficit brought forward £12.396m, in-year deficit £10.099m, deficit carried forward £22.495m. High needs overspend £5.242m.
findings.quote: The budget for centrally-managed items in the DSG envisaged an in-year deficit in 2025/26 of £5.893m. Compared to this Bexley's final outturn was a deficit of £10.099m, therefore representing a net adverse variance of £4.206m.

findings.paper_title: 7.1 26 LBB 225UK Audit Planning Report - Local Government 2025-26
findings.headline: Auditors signaled they may invoke statutory powers if Council's financial reporting arrangements are inadequate
findings.detail: Auditors explicitly stated they will 'consider the use of other statutory reporting powers to draw attention to weaknesses in Council financial reporting arrangements, where deemed necessary' if the Council fails to provide quality working papers, resources, and compliance with agreed deadlines. This threat signals auditors view governance risks as material.
findings.matters: Statutory reporting powers are invoked for significant failures in financial reporting governance; this flag indicates auditors have assessed a material risk that the council may not support timely and reliable accounting.
findings.figures: No figures
findings.quote: Consider the use of other statutory reporting powers to draw attention to weaknesses in Council financial reporting arrangements, where deemed necessary.

findings.paper_title: 7.1 26 LBB 225UK Audit Planning Report - Local Government 2025-26
findings.headline: Auditors cannot rebuild assurance over historical asset valuations and reserves; waiting for external guidance
findings.detail: Auditors are explicitly unable to commence work rebuilding assurance over Property, Plant & Equipment, PFI, IFRS16, Reserves, and Group Statements affected by the 2024-25 disclaimer. They are waiting for guidance from the National Audit Office and Financial Reporting Council; until then, the assurance gap remains unaddressed and opening balances for 2025-26 will be unaudited.
findings.matters: If opening asset valuations and reserve positions cannot be audited, the council's starting financial position is unverified, limiting the reliability of all subsequent balance sheet and reserve figures.
findings.figures: No figures
findings.quote: Restoring assurance will need local authorities and auditors to work together. We are waiting for guidance from the National Audit Office and Financial Reporting Council to ensure a consistent approach for restoring assurance for disclaimed periods. Until then, we are unable to commence the rebuilding work programme.

findings.paper_title: 7.1 26 LBB 225UK Audit Planning Report - Local Government 2025-26
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease and PFI accounting issues unresolved after 2024-25 audit; elevated to significant risk
findings.detail: Auditors were unable to complete 2024-25 procedures on IFRS 16 Leases due to outstanding questions about the PFI model and lease accounting. They have elevated this to a significant risk area and engaged an internal specialist to perform a specific review in March 2026, indicating material accounting problems remain unresolved.
findings.matters: IFRS 16 requires all lease obligations to be recognised on the balance sheet as right-of-use assets and liabilities; unresolved PFI accounting directly misrepresents the true liability position that lenders and finance directors evaluate.
findings.figures: No amounts disclosed for unresolved IFRS 16 or PFI balances
findings.quote: We were unable to complete the planned 2024/25 audit procedures for this account, due to number of outstanding questions raised in relation to PFI model and underlying lease accounting as at completion of the audit. We have decided to increase the risk to significant risk area to reflect the prior year issues

findings.paper_title: 7.1 26 LBB 225UK Audit Planning Report - Local Government 2025-26
findings.headline: Bexley's 2024-25 accounts received a disclaimed audit opinion; 2025-26 may face the same outcome
findings.detail: The auditors disclaimed their audit opinion on 2024-25 financial statements because they lacked assurance over brought-forward balances including Property, Plant & Equipment, PFI, IFRS16 disclosures, Reserves, and Group Statements. For 2025-26, they expect to audit only closing balances and in-year movements but explicitly state they cannot obtain sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all closing balances, and will assess whether to issue another disclaimer or qualified opinion.
findings.matters: A disclaimed or qualified audit opinion means external assurance over the financial position is unreliable; lenders depend on audited accounts to assess credit risk, and the finance director cannot report a true financial position to the council.
findings.figures: Gross expenditure on provision of services: £586m; Planning materiality: £10.5m (1.8% of gross expenditure)
findings.quote: Although we will continue to work towards rebuilding assurance ahead of the 2025/26 backstop date (subject to guidance), we will not be able to obtain sufficient evidence to have reasonable assurance over all closing balances. In undertaking our planned procedures we will assess if it will again be appropriate to issue a disclaimer of opinion in 2025/26 or whether we can move to a qualified opinion.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 25 LBB LG Auditors Annual Report 24-25
findings.headline: Contract inflation pressures: 51.57% of council budget spent on supplies and services, with inflation continuing
findings.detail: The council reports that it spends 51.57% of its budget on supplies and services and third-party contracts, making it vulnerable to contract inflation. Even with inflation rates reduced from their peaks, this remains a material budget pressure identified in the MTFS.
findings.matters: Over half the council's budget is exposed to contract inflation risk, which the council cannot fully control. This is a source of unplanned budget pressure.
findings.figures: 51.57% of budget on supplies and services and third party contracts
findings.quote: the Council spends 51.57% of the budget on supplies and services and third party contracts

findings.paper_title: 6.1 25 LBB LG Auditors Annual Report 24-25
findings.headline: LGA peer review raised concerns over low revenue reserves and trending overspends in social services
findings.detail: The LGA peer review (conducted January 2025, reported March 2025) identified concerns about the council's financial sustainability due to low revenue reserves and trending overspends in both Adults and Children's services. The review also flagged overreliance on transformation to balance the MTFS without clear link to corporate strategy or value-for-money outcomes.
findings.matters: Independent external review by LGA flagged the same structural issues (reserves, social care overspends) that a lender would identify as risk factors. Twelve recommendations were made; the council accepted all but implementation risk remains.
findings.figures: 12 LGA recommendations made; all accepted
findings.quote: Concerns over the Council's financial sustainability were raised with the low level of revenue reserves and the trending overspends in Adults and Children's services.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 25 LBB LG Auditors Annual Report 24-25
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting for PFI arrangements remains unresolved and will remain unaudited
findings.detail: EY has identified ongoing questions in relation to the council's PFI model and underlying lease accounting under IFRS 16. The auditor states it is "unlikely that we will conclude our work in this area before the backstop" and the balances will be included as unaudited in the disclaimer report. This represents a gap in audit coverage for an undefined balance.
findings.matters: An unaudited PFI/lease balance means the council's liabilities may be understated or overstated without audit verification, affecting borrowing capacity assessment and debt position.
findings.figures: IFRS 16 leases work incomplete at backstop date
findings.quote: It is unlikely that we will conclude our work in this area before the backstop and the balances will be included in our disclaimer audit report as unaudited in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 25 LBB LG Auditors Annual Report 24-25
findings.headline: Property valuations contain material errors: Broadway Shopping Centre reduced by £9.9 million total
findings.detail: EY testing identified a reduction in Broadway Shopping Centre value of £4.4m due to yield assumption changes, plus a further £5.5m adjustment because the council's valuer had used incorrect yield values. These are unadjusted differences in the financial statements, indicating control weaknesses in asset valuation.
findings.matters: Material valuation errors on investment property suggest inadequate controls over estimates and raise questions about the reliability of other property valuations on the balance sheet.
findings.figures: £4.4m reduction from yield assumption changes, £5.5m from valuer error, total £9.9m
findings.quote: Our testing has highlighted a reduction in the value of Broadway Shopping Centre of £4.4m as a result of changes in yield assumptions and a further adjustment of £5.5 million where the valuer had used the incorrect yield values.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 25 LBB LG Auditors Annual Report 24-25
findings.headline: Usable reserves forecast to decline significantly across the medium term
findings.detail: The audit report charts show both General Reserve and earmarked reserves falling from 2024/25 through 2028/29. The council plans to maintain the general reserve at £14m but the overall reserve position is deteriorating as mitigations for overspends consume earmarked reserves.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce the council's ability to absorb unexpected shocks or fund one-off service pressures, increasing financial fragility.
findings.figures: General Reserve targeted at £14m; earmarked reserves declining
findings.quote: The Council's usable reserve continue to fall

findings.paper_title: 6.1 25 LBB LG Auditors Annual Report 24-25
findings.headline: Overall council overspend of £1.5 million funded by drawing down the Financial Planning reserve
findings.detail: After all directorate variances, the council recorded a net overspend of £1.5m in 2024/25 and funded this by drawing on reserves rather than staying within budget. The report states that "mitigations and savings will need to be found in 2025/26 to prevent a further realisation of these pressures."
findings.matters: The council is consuming reserves to manage operational overspends, reducing its financial buffer year on year. This is unsustainable if structural pressures continue.
findings.figures: £1.5m overspend funded from Financial Planning reserve
findings.quote: For 2024/25, the resulting overspend has been funded from the Financial Planning reserve.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 25 LBB LG Auditors Annual Report 24-25
findings.headline: Adult social care overspent by £2.5 million in 2024/25
findings.detail: Adult Social Care and Public Health outturn was £80.2m against a budget of £77.7m. The council reports facing increasing levels of demand, higher unit costs, and greater competition in this demand-led service. This is the council's largest directorate budget and another key pressure area.
findings.matters: Adult social care is the largest directorate budget and nationally is driving cost pressures across local government. Inability to hold budget here indicates structural demand pressures.
findings.figures: Budget £77.7m, outturn £80.2m, overspend £2.5m
findings.quote: Adult Social Care and Public Health 77.7 80.2 2.5

findings.paper_title: 6.1 25 LBB LG Auditors Annual Report 24-25
findings.headline: Children's services overspent by £4.9 million in 2024/25, the largest directorate overspend
findings.detail: Children and Education outturn was £60.4m against a budget of £55.5m, a 9% overspend. This is a demand-led service where the council faces increasing demand, higher unit costs, and competition for placements. The overspend was not contained within the directorate budget.
findings.matters: Children's services is the second-largest directorate budget and is one of the fastest-growing demand pressures nationally. Inability to manage spend here signals loss of budget control in a high-volatility area.
findings.figures: Budget £55.5m, outturn £60.4m, overspend £4.9m
findings.quote: Children and Education 55.5 60.4 4.9

findings.paper_title: 6.1 25 LBB LG Auditors Annual Report 24-25
findings.headline: Council achieved only 84% of planned savings in 2024/25, underfunding by £1.5 million
findings.detail: The council planned to deliver £9.5m of savings but achieved only £8.0m. Significant shortfalls occurred in Children's (£1.2m) due to commissioning alliance benefits not being realised, and Place (£1.0m) due to parking review delays and inadequate resourcing. This shortfall directly funded an operating overspend.
findings.matters: Demonstrates delivery risk on savings plans, which the council relies on heavily to address its structural budget gap. Successive years of shortfalls are a leading indicator of financial distress.
findings.figures: £8.0m achieved of £9.5m planned (84%); Children's shortfall £1.2m, Place shortfall £1.0m
findings.quote: The Council delivered 84% of planned £9.5 million of savings in 2024/25

findings.paper_title: 6.1 25 LBB LG Auditors Annual Report 24-25
findings.headline: Structural budget gap of £49.542 million by 2029/30, with no solution yet identified
findings.detail: The council's Medium Term Financial Strategy identifies a budget gap rising from £32.658m in 2026/27 to £49.542m by 2029/30. The primary mitigation is a transformation programme with undefined savings. The LGA peer review expressed concern about overreliance on transformation as the sole mechanism to balance the budget.
findings.matters: A lender faces risk of a council unable to deliver balanced budgets across the planning horizon, potentially leading to service cuts, tax rises, or further borrowing.
findings.quote: the Council now has a budget gap of £32.658m for 2026/27 increasing to £49.542m by 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 25 LBB LG Auditors Annual Report 24-25
findings.headline: Disclaimer of opinion on 2024/25 financial statements due to insufficient audit evidence
findings.detail: EY issued a disclaimed audit opinion on 17 February 2026, unable to obtain sufficient evidence over all in-year movements and closing balances. The disclaimer carries forward from 2023/24, meaning the council has now been unable to produce auditable accounts for two consecutive years. This prevents the council from issuing a clean financial certificate.
findings.matters: A lender cannot validate the council's true financial position, asset values, or liabilities. This is a fundamental control failure that affects all financial decision-making.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinion issued 17 February 2026 for year ended 31 March 2025
findings.quote: We therefore issued a disclaimed 2024/25 audit opinion on 17 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Feb 2026 - Treasury Management Strategy - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Council deliberately under-borrowing by using cash reserves as temporary funding pending interest rate falls
findings.detail: Rather than borrowing to fund its full Capital Financing Requirement, the council is using cash from its reserves and balances as a temporary measure. This strategy is described as prudent only because the council expects interest rates to fall. If rates do not fall as forecast, this temporary approach will require reversal, either through higher-cost borrowing or drawdown of reserve funds.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council's current liquidity position is contingent on reserves and dependent on specific interest rate forecasts. If strategy must change, it could significantly impact reserve levels and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Treasury investments £20.329m; external borrowing £227.599m (as at 31.12.2025); net position (£207.271m)
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position.  This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Feb 2026 - Treasury Management Strategy - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement will increase by £74.5 million over three years, a 17 per cent rise
findings.detail: Total CFR rises from £436.259m in 2026/27 to £510.766m by 2028/29, driven primarily by Bexley Company's planned capital programme. This reflects a substantial increase in the council's underlying borrowing need and future annual debt service costs.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's finances needs to understand that the council is taking on significantly higher capital commitments that will require new borrowing and increase annual debt service obligations.

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Feb 2026 - Treasury Management Strategy - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Borrowing strategy depends on interest rates falling, but forecast risks are acknowledged to be upside
findings.detail: The council is maintaining an under-borrowed position based on MUFG's forecast that PWLB rates will fall from current 4.81% (5-year rate) to a target of 4.10%. However, the strategy explicitly states that risks to these forecasts are to the upside, meaning if rates remain higher than forecast, the cost of the planned £144m borrowing programme could increase significantly beyond budget assumptions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's financial plan depends on specific interest rate forecasts being correct. If those assumptions prove wrong and rates remain elevated or rise further, the cost of the planned borrowing programme will exceed projections.
findings.figures: Current 5-year PWLB rate 4.81%; target rate 4.10%
findings.quote: but the risks to these forecasts are generally to the upside

findings.paper_title: Appendix J - Feb 2026 - Treasury Management Strategy - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Bexley Company will borrow £144 million over three years; investment purpose is not explained in this document
findings.detail: The company's debt is projected to grow from £40.234m to £179.663m by 2029/30, driven by planned new borrowing of £67.034m in 2026/27, £47.056m in 2027/28, and £30.000m in 2028/29. The Treasury Strategy does not identify what capital projects or investments this borrowing will fund. The company's CFR alone will account for most of the council's total CFR growth over the period.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand why the council is taking on £144 million of new debt through a company vehicle over three years to assess whether it is sustainable and whether the returns justify the investment.
findings.figures: £67.034m, £47.056m, £30.000m (new borrowing by year); Bexley Co projected CFR £179.663m by 2029/30; total CFR grows from £436.259m to £510.766m
findings.quote: Bexley Co - New Borrowing 67.034  47.056  30.000  -

findings.paper_title: Appendix H - Feb 2026 - Capital Strategy - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Council explicitly identifies limited reserves as a constraint on its ability to absorb capital cost variations or project delivery failures.
findings.detail: In the Risk Management section, the council flags funding risk as 'a significant risk to the council given the limited reserves available and implications of increasing borrowing'. This is a direct statement that reserves provide insufficient buffer against cost overruns on the £253m capital programme or delivery shortfalls on the BexleyCo schemes that the entire financial strategy depends on.
findings.matters: Thin reserves mean the council has limited ability to absorb project overruns, scope changes, or underperformance without cascading effects on the revenue budget or service provision.
findings.figures: Capital programme: £145.339m (2026/27), rising to £253.008m total; 90% funded by borrowing
findings.quote: Funding risk – Variations in the cost of a project or non-delivery of the expected outcomes could be a significant risk to the council given the limited reserves available and implications of increasing borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H - Feb 2026 - Capital Strategy - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Total debt financing costs rising to 12.12% of net revenue by 2029/30, reaching the upper end of the council's 10-15% prudence range.
findings.detail: The council's financing cost ratio (debt servicing as a percentage of revenue) is projected to rise from 9.51% in 2026/27 to 12.12% by 2029/30. This approaches the upper limit of the 10-15% range that the Director of Finance has advised as prudent strategy. Of this, BexleyCo's financing costs alone grow from 1.59% to 3.92%. This shows accelerating debt servicing burdens relative to available revenue.
findings.matters: Rising debt servicing costs leave the council with less revenue flexibility for service delivery or responding to unexpected pressures. Reaching 12.12% leaves limited headroom if interest rates rise or BexleyCo revenues disappoint.
findings.quote: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream for each year is estimated in the following tables for each method. It should be noted that loans to BexleyCo are repayable during the period. There is no set rule for the ratio, however the Director of Finance & Corporate Services has advised a prudent strategy for this would be between 10% and 15%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix H - Feb 2026 - Capital Strategy - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: £144m BexleyCo regeneration programme entirely borrowing-funded, with council explicitly flagging income delivery as critical to financial sustainability.
findings.detail: The council plans £144.090m capital investment in BexleyCo (its property development company) over 4 years, all financed by borrowing. The strategy explicitly states that 'delivery of income streams due from the series of Regeneration led projects for housing development are crucial and underpin the Council's ability to meet the cost of this capital investment and generate future revenue returns to support the delivery of the Medium-Term Financial Strategy'. The document warns: 'Failure to deliver to plan, could result in significant financial pressures for the Council'.
findings.matters: This reveals the council's financial strategy is contingent on a development company delivering income, not just capital returns. If BexleyCo projects underperform on revenue generation, the council faces direct pressure on its MTFS and its ability to fund services.
findings.figures: £144.090m total BexleyCo investment (2026/27-2029/30); £67.034m in 2026/27 alone; all funded by borrowing
findings.quote: In particular, the delivery of income streams due from the series of Regeneration led projects for housing development are crucial and underpin the Council's ability to meet the cost of this capital investment and generate future revenue returns to support the delivery of the Medium-Term Financial Strategy. Failure to deliver to plan, could result in significant financial pressures for the Council

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Feb 2026- Section 25 Statement - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Income pressures: council is seeing reduction in both income levels and collection rates, whilst costs inflate
findings.detail: The s151 officer lists as an ongoing challenge: 'See a reduction in both income levels and collection rates.' This occurs against a backdrop of inflationary pressures on service costs (contract and pay inflation), creating a squeeze: revenue is falling or stagnant whilst costs rise. The document also cites 'the cost of living pressures faced by residents' as a risk factor, which will further depress collection rates and demand for council services.
findings.matters: Falling income combined with rising costs is the core definition of financial stress. Collection rate decline is a leading indicator of resident financial hardship and signals future revenue stability risk.
findings.figures: None stated quantitatively; noted as an ongoing pressure
findings.quote: See a reduction in both income levels and collection rates; the cost of living pressures faced by residents.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Feb 2026- Section 25 Statement - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Limited capital asset base restricts capital receipts; borrowing (£227.559m) expected to increase further across medium term
findings.detail: The council has 'a limited asset base and therefore reduced opportunity to receive capital receipts.' This constrains flexibility: capital schemes cannot be funded from asset sales, so borrowing must increase. Current borrowing stands at £227.559m with 11% maturing in the medium term. The s151 officer expects 'the level of borrowing will increase and the capital programme will need to be closely managed to keep the cost of borrowing under 15%.'
findings.matters: Rising debt with limited tangible assets to offset it increases leverage and interest expense. A lender assesses debt-to-asset ratios; limited receipts mean borrowing grows faster than assets and the council's balance sheet becomes more leveraged.
findings.figures: Current borrowing £227.559m, 11% due to mature medium term, cost of borrowing target under 15%
findings.quote: The Council has a limited asset base and therefore reduced opportunity to receive capital receipts. This results in the Council being more reliant on borrowing to support the capital programme...The level of borrowing is currently £227.559m with 11% due to mature over the medium term. Across the medium term it is expected the level of borrowing will increase.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Feb 2026- Section 25 Statement - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Social care demand and complexity pressures continue, with recruitment and agency staff challenges pushing costs higher
findings.detail: Social care (adults and children) consumes 74% of the council's net revenue budget and is flagged as a demand-led area with 'increased levels of demand and increased complexity of need.' The council faces 'recruitment and retention challenges of staff, specifically in relation to Social Care and professional service where there is an increasing level and cost of agency staff.' The budget has been grown to accommodate these pressures, but the document flags this as an ongoing and unpredictable challenge.
findings.matters: Demand-led services cannot be arbitrarily cut. A council spending 74% of revenue on social care has limited flexibility. Rising complexity and agency costs are structural pressures; if unfunded growth exceeds budget, the council must find savings elsewhere or draw reserves.
findings.figures: 74% of net revenue expenditure on social care
findings.quote: Social Care services (both Adults Services and Children's Services) and SEN Transport have seen increased levels of demand and increased costs requiring increased budgetary provision...Face recruitment and retention challenges of staff, specifically in relation to Social Care and professional service where there is an increasing level and cost of agency staff.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Feb 2026- Section 25 Statement - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Contract inflation pressure: 52% of revenue budget is outsourced, with £10.572m set aside but risk of provider claims exceeding allocation
findings.detail: Over half the council's revenue budget (approximately 52%) goes to third-party supplies and services. The council has set aside £10.572m for contract inflation, but many contracts are index-linked to RPI or CPI and the s151 officer acknowledges 'there is the risk that providers will seek increases in excess of that set aside.' Mitigation relies on contract renegotiation, which 'in some areas opportunities will be limited.'
findings.matters: Market-driven inflation on outsourced services is outside council control. If providers demand more than budgeted, the council either finds additional cash or cuts service provision. This is a material exposure for a lender evaluating financial resilience.
findings.figures: 52% of net revenue budget spent on third parties, £10.572m inflation provision
findings.quote: The Council spends approximately 52% of its revenue budget on third party supplies and services as most services are outsourced and therefore at greater risk of high contract inflation...There is the risk that providers will seek increases in excess of that set aside to cover the living wage and Employer NI increases.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Feb 2026- Section 25 Statement - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget balanced using one-off reserve releases, which the s151 officer states is 'clearly not sustainable'
findings.detail: To achieve a balanced 2026/27 budget, the council deployed one-off releases from reserves 'held for purposes that following assessment are no longer required.' The s151 officer explicitly signals this approach cannot continue: 'Although overreliance has not been placed on reserves, the use of one-off monies is clearly not sustainable.' This flags a structural gap between recurring revenue and recurring expenditure.
findings.matters: Using reserves to balance the current budget year indicates the recurring budget is in deficit. Reserves should cushion shocks, not fund operations. Once-only resources are finite; continued reliance signals deteriorating underlying position.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves forecast at £48.315m at end of 2026/27
findings.quote: it has been necessary to deploy one off resources by way of release of specific reserves held for purposes that following assessment are no longer required. Although overreliance has not been placed on reserves, the use of one-off monies is clearly not sustainable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Feb 2026- Section 25 Statement - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Council tax dependency rising to 63.7% by 2028/29, up from 58.8%, creating vulnerability to collection and resistance
findings.detail: Council tax is becoming an increasingly dominant funding source. The s151 officer explicitly states this shift 'presents a risk for the Council moving forward' and insists maximum allowed increases 'should always be levied.' This concentration creates vulnerability: collection rates are falling per the budget document, and resident cost-of-living pressures are noted as a risk factor.
findings.matters: Rising dependency on council tax increases vulnerability to collection failures, resident resistance at higher rates, and economic downturns. A lender assessing repayment capacity needs stable revenue; concentration in one volatile source is a weakness.
findings.quote: the overall dependency on Council Tax is forecast to increase from current levels of 58.8% in 2025/26 to a level of 63.7% by 2028/29. Given the sustained increase building on from previous years, the preservation of the Council Tax from a revenue generation perspective must be maintained and the maximum increases as permitted through the Local Government Finance Settlement should always be levied.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Feb 2026- Section 25 Statement - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: SEND deficit of £24m+ now partially funded by government but council retains 10% liability
findings.detail: The council faces a Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of over £24m by end of 2025/26. New government grant will cover 90% of High Needs-related deficits accrued to end of 2025/26, but the council must fund the remaining 10%. For deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28, the government letter indicates support will continue but 'will not be unlimited.' This quantifies a previously unquantified risk but leaves ongoing exposure.
findings.matters: SEND deficits reflect real, rising demand that cannot be controlled. A council bearing even 10% of a £24m+ deficit has material liability; future deficits beyond the cap create open-ended exposure.
findings.figures: SEND deficit in excess of £24m, 90% government funded from 2026/27, council funds 10%
findings.quote: For the Council that deficit is projected to be in excess of £24m by the end of 2025/26 financial year...local authorities with SEND deficits will be eligible in 2026 /27 to receive a grant covering 90% of their High Needs-related DSG deficit accrued up to the end of 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Feb 2026- Section 25 Statement - Public Cabinet
findings.headline: Budget gaps of £17.8m by 2029/30 emerging across the medium term despite a balanced 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: After balancing 2026/27, the council faces projected budget gaps of £8.192m in 2027/28 rising to £17.815m by 2029/30. The s151 officer acknowledges these are 'not to be dismissed' and will require continued transformation and new income generation. The council's ability to close these gaps has not yet been demonstrated.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can deliver £17.8m of savings in three years whilst maintaining service quality. These forward gaps indicate structural imbalance, not temporary pressures.
findings.quote: The Councils current financial plans propose a balanced budget for 2026/27 with subsequent budget gaps from 2027/28 of £8.192m rising through £17.815m by 2029/30.

findings.committee: Finance & Corporate Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: TMS Report
findings.headline: BexleyCo capital investments growing from £40m to £181m over four years, requiring sustained high-level borrowing
findings.detail: The council's capital company CFR is forecast to grow more than fourfold, from £40.2m (opening 2026/27) to £181.5m by 2028/29, driven by new borrowing of £67m, £47m, and £30m across three years. Nature and detailed risks of these capital investments are not specified in this strategy (see Capital Strategy for details).
findings.matters: Represents significant capital commitments by council-controlled company; service delivery depends on these projects performing; council is exposed to capital project risks and cost overruns
findings.figures: BexleyCo CFR 2026/27 £106.8m, growing to £181.479m by 2028/29; new borrowing £67.034m + £47.056m + £30.000m = £144.09m over three years

findings.committee: Finance & Corporate Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: TMS Report
findings.headline: Borrowing plans are contingent on interest rates falling from current levels; if rates rise, capital scheme costs will exceed budget
findings.detail: The council will only proceed with planned borrowing if rates fall as forecast (5yr PWLB currently 4.81%, target 4.10% by end 2027). If actual rates are higher than the MUFG forecast, the council will face higher debt servicing costs. The strategy explicitly reserves the right to accelerate borrowing if rates spike, creating execution risk.
findings.matters: Exposes council to interest rate risk; capital programme affordability is dependent on advisor forecasts that may not materialise; potential for cost inflation if borrowing markets tighten
findings.figures: Current 5yr PWLB 4.81%; MUFG target rate end Q4 2027: 4.10%; Bank Rate forecast low 3.25% in 2027
findings.quote: if it was felt that there was a significant risk of a much sharper RISE in borrowing rates than that currently forecast, fixed rate funding will be drawn whilst interest rates are lower than they are projected to be in the next few years.

findings.committee: Finance & Corporate Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: TMS Report
findings.headline: Council is using reserves and cash balances to finance capital spending rather than borrowing, exposing future liquidity
findings.detail: Current outstanding debt is £227.6m against a CFR of £436.3m, leaving a £208.7m gap being financed from reserves. This under-borrowed position is a temporary strategy while the council waits for interest rates to fall. When capital plans require actual borrowing, liquidity will be affected.
findings.matters: Depletes reserves that the council may need for other purposes or contingencies; indicates larger underlying borrowing need than current debt suggests
findings.figures: Outstanding debt 31 Dec 2025: £227.599m; CFR 2026/27: £436.334m; gap of £208.735m
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position.  This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.committee: Finance & Corporate Services Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: TMS Report
findings.headline: Council is planning £117m of new borrowing in 2026/27, with total Capital Financing Requirement growing to £510m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The council's CFR grows from £436.3m in 2026/27 to £510.2m by 2028/29. New borrowing planned is £50.3m for General Fund and £67m for BexleyCo in 2026/27 alone, declining over subsequent years. This represents sustained capital investment commitments.
findings.matters: Material increase in the council's total indebtedness and annual borrowing requirement; any slippage in capital receipts or revenue income could constrain ability to service growing debt
